desc:
A map grid has 0 for water and 1 for land. The distance between two cells at (r1, c1) and (r2, c2) is |r1 - r2| + |c1 - c2|, which is the number of up/down/left/right steps between them.

Find the water cell whose distance to the closest land cell is as large as possible, and return that distance. If the map has no water or no land at all, return -1.

grid = [[1,0,1],
        [0,0,0],
        [1,0,1]]  -> 2

grid = [[1,0,0],
        [0,0,0],
        [0,0,0]]  -> 4

In the first map the middle cell is two steps from every corner; in the second the opposite corner is four steps from the only land cell.
hints: First deal with the degenerate maps (all water or all land). Then think about what 'closest land' means for all water cells simultaneously.
Compute, for every water cell, its distance to the nearest land cell with one BFS that starts from all land cells together.
BFS visits cells in nondecreasing distance, so the distance of the last cell taken from the queue is the maximum. No separate max tracking is needed.
editorial: If there is no land or no water, return -1. Otherwise push all land cells into a queue with distance 0 and run a BFS over the whole grid (no obstacles exist, so every cell is reachable). Each water cell gets the distance of the first wave that reaches it, which is its distance to the nearest land.

The answer is the largest distance assigned. Since cells leave the queue in order of increasing distance, the final popped cell has the maximum. This runs in O(rows × cols); the naive approach of comparing every water cell with every land cell is quadratic in the number of cells.
